query: For a damaged high-value component made from a material whose physical and microstructural characteristics make traditional fusion-welding repair ineffective because of hot-cracking risk, what intervention could enable continued service without replacing the entire part under aggressive operating conditions? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to traditional fusion-welding repair, the relevant operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Utilizing friction stir processing (FSP) as a localized repair intervention on the damaged high-value component will mitigate hot-cracking risks by avoiding melting and solidification, while simultaneously refining the microstructure to restore or even enhance the mechanical performance relative to traditional fusion-weld repairs.
generation.material_initial_state: The component is made from a material (e.g., an aluminum alloy or a high-entropy alloy composite) with a microstructure that is highly susceptible to hot-cracking when exposed to fusion-welding thermal cycles.
generation.intervention: Apply friction stir processing to the damaged region, optionally incorporating high-entropy alloy (HEA) reinforcement particles to achieve a graded, dual-layered core–shell interfacial structure.
generation.conditions: The intervention is implemented under aggressive operating conditions where the component is subjected to high thermal gradients and cyclic mechanical loads, similar to those in severe aerospace or high-performance applications.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a refined, dual-layered interface (with a gradient composition, such as an inner region rich in HEA particles and an outer layer tailored by subsequent heat treatment) that reduces residual stresses and blocks crack initiation.
generation.mechanism: FSP induces severe plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization eliminating the melting phase, thereby avoiding the formation of solidification-induced hot cracks. Additionally, controlled heat treatment post-FSP promotes a gradual compositional and microstructural transition at the repair interface, enhancing bonding and toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: The FSP-repaired area will exhibit improved tensile strength and ductility with a significantly reduced propensity for hot cracking compared to conventional fusion-welded joints, leading to a longer service life under aggressive conditions.
generation.baseline: Traditional fusion-welding repairs of this material typically lead to hot-cracking and inferior mechanical properties due to the rapid solidification process and high thermal stresses.
generation.boundary: This repair method is expected to be effective provided the operating temperatures remain below the tool limits for FSP, and the material system is similar to those studied in friction stir processed aluminum alloy/HEA composites and non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys.
generation.uncertainty: It remains uncertain how well the FSP repair technique scales to components with complex geometries or varied damage profiles, and whether the incorporation of HEA particles consistently improves the interfacial bonding across different material systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens from the same damaged high-value component material. One set will undergo traditional fusion-welding repair while the other is repaired using friction stir processing (with and without the incorporation of HEA particles). Both sets are then subjected to aggressive thermal cycling and mechanical loading designed to simulate operating conditions.
measurements: Microstructural characterization via optical and electron microscopy to assess grain structure and detect hot-cracks.
Mechanical testing such as tensile strength, ductility, and fatigue resistance.
Residual stress analysis across the repaired zones.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the FSP-repaired specimens show no significant reduction in hot-cracking, do not exhibit improved or equivalent mechanical properties compared to fusion-welded specimens, or if they develop new kinds of failure under the aggressive test conditions, the hypothesis would be considered falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractEquiatomic AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) has gained significant interest in recent years because of its excellent mechanical properties. A356 aluminum alloy reinforced by AlCoCrFeNi HEA particles was fabricated by friction stir processing (FSP) and subsequent heat treatment. Solution and aging treatments were specially performed for the composites to control the interface microstructure, and interfacial microstructure and tensile properties were explored at different conditions. The interface between the matrix and HEA particles showed a dual-layered core–shell structure and the thickness of the shell region increased with the solution time. The microstructure located in the shell layers consisted of a solid solution with increasing aluminum content, in which a radial-shaped solid solution phase formed in the region close to the core of the HEA particle and scattered solid solution grains with high Ni content formed in the region close to the matrix alloy. ## Abstract
AbstractTo study the thermal cracking susceptibility of laser-welded CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloys, stainless steel and aluminum alloy plates were each used as backing for welding. The microstructure of the weld and morphology of the fracture were examined. In addition, the chemical compositions of the fractures, the interfacial tension between the CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy and liquid aluminum alloy, and the linear expansion coefficient of the CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy were determined. The results show that when stainless steel is used as the base plate, no cracking is apparent in the weld, and the microstructure is made up of dendrites and equiaxed crystals. Conversely, when an aluminum alloy plate is adopted, solidification cracks are seen at the center of the weld, and the microstructure consists of bright polygonal dendrites scattered in a dark gray matrix. ## Abstract
AbstractThe potential of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to exhibit an extraordinary combination of properties by shifting the compositional regime from the corners towards the centers of phase diagrams has led to worldwide attention by material scientists. Here we present a strong and ductile non-equiatomic HEA obtained after friction stir processing (FSP). A transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) assisted HEA with composition Fe50Mn30Co10Cr10 (at.%) was severely deformed by FSP and evaluated for its microstructure-mechanical property relationship. The FSP-engineered microstructure of the TRIP HEA exhibited a substantially smaller grain size, and optimized fractions of face-centered cubic (f.c.c., γ) and hexagonal close-packed (h.c.p., ε) phases, as compared to the as-homogenized reference material. This results in synergistic strengthening via TRIP, grain boundary strengthening, and effective strain partitioning between the γ and ε phases during deformation, thus leading to enhanced strength and ductility of the TRIP-assisted dual-phase HEA engineered via FSP.
